title: THE DAY GOD TRIED TO KILL MOSES
paragraphs: THE DAY GOD TRIED TO KILL MOSES
Some passages in Scripture feel safe.
Others feel uncomfortable.
And then there are passages that stop you cold.
Passages that seem to shatter everything you thought you understood about God.
Exodus 4:24 is one of them.
“On the way, at a lodging place, the LORD met him and sought to put him to death.”
That is not a verse most people frame on their wall.
God had just called Moses from the burning bush.
God had chosen him.
Commissioned him.
Empowered him.
Promised to use him to confront Pharaoh and liberate Israel.
Yet suddenly, in the darkness of a desert journey, God Himself appears ready to kill the very man He had chosen.
Why?
What happened between the burning bush and Egypt?
Why would the God who called Moses now stand against him?
And what does this terrifying encounter reveal about our own lives today?
To understand the moment, we must first understand the man.
Moses was not standing before God as a perfect servant.
He was a complicated mixture of faith and failure.
Raised in Pharaoh’s palace.
A Hebrew by birth.
An Egyptian by culture.
A fugitive by circumstance.
A shepherd by necessity.
For forty years he had lived in Midian after killing an Egyptian.
Then God interrupted everything.
From the flames of the bush, God declared His covenant faithfulness and His intention to rescue Israel.
Moses resisted repeatedly.
“Who am I?”
“What if they don't believe me?”
“What if I cannot speak?”
“Send someone else.”
Yet despite all his objections, God remained patient.
Merciful.
Persistent.
The mission was clear.
Moses would lead God's people out of bondage.
But there was one hidden problem.
A private act of disobedience.
Something Moses had apparently tolerated for years.
Something no one in Egypt knew.
Something that would never appear on a résumé.
His son had not been circumcised.
At first glance, that may seem insignificant to modern readers.
But in Scripture, circumcision was never merely a medical procedure.
It was covenant identity.
It was the sign God gave Abraham.
Genesis 17:10 records God's command:
“This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your offspring after you: Every male among you shall be circumcised.”
The Hebrew word for covenant is בְּרִית (berith).
A covenant was not a casual agreement.
It was a binding relationship established by God Himself.
To reject the covenant sign was to reject covenant loyalty.
Genesis 17:14 is even more direct:
“Any uncircumcised male... shall be cut off from his people; he has broken my covenant.”
Moses was about to represent God's covenant before an entire nation.
Yet apparently he was neglecting the covenant within his own household.
The issue was not merely external ritual.
The issue was obedience.
Integrity.
Submission.
The issue was whether the messenger himself would bow before the message he carried.
Then comes the shocking confrontation.
Exodus 4:24 states:
וַיִּפְגְּשֵׁהוּ יְהוָה וַיְבַקֵּשׁ הֲמִיתוֹ
Vayyifgeshehu Adonai vayevakkesh hamito.
“The LORD met him and sought to kill him.”
The Hebrew language intentionally communicates danger and urgency.
God is not playing games.
This is not symbolic.
This is covenant seriousness.
The God of grace is also the God of holiness.
The God who delivers slaves is also the God who refuses compromise.
Many believers love God's calling.
Far fewer love God's authority.
We celebrate destiny.
We celebrate purpose.
We celebrate blessing.
But covenant obedience is often where enthusiasm disappears.
Yet Scripture repeatedly reveals a sobering truth.
God cares more about our character than our platform.
More about our obedience than our influence.
More about holiness than visibility.
Moses was chosen.
But being chosen did not exempt him from accountability.
In fact, it increased it.
Then Zipporah enters the story.
Exodus 4:25 says:
“Then Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son's foreskin and touched Moses' feet with it and said, ‘Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me!’”
The details are mysterious.
Scholars debate several elements of the passage.
But the central point remains unmistakable.
The covenant sign was finally administered.
Obedience occurred.
Judgment was averted.
And Moses lived.
The entire encounter exposes a reality many modern Christians desperately need to hear.
Private disobedience eventually collides with public calling.
God is not impressed by ministry while covenant faithfulness is neglected.
The Lord who sees the crowds also sees the secrets.
The Lord who opens doors also examines hearts.
The Lord who appoints leaders also disciplines His children.
The frightening scene at the lodging place is not evidence of divine cruelty.
It is evidence of divine consistency.
God was preparing Moses for one of the greatest assignments in redemptive history.
And before confronting Pharaoh, Moses himself had to be confronted.
Before leading a nation, he had to submit.
Before delivering others, he had to obey.
This pattern echoes throughout Scripture.
Jacob wrestled before he walked differently.
Isaiah was cleansed before he preached.
Peter was broken before he strengthened his brothers.
Paul was blinded before he truly saw.
God often does His deepest work in private places long before He works through us publicly.
And perhaps that is why this strange story remains so relevant.
Many people today want God to change their circumstances.
But God first wants to transform them.
We ask Him to bless our plans.
He asks us to surrender our hearts.
We ask Him for influence.
He asks for obedience.
We ask Him for platforms.
He asks for holiness.
We ask Him to rewrite our story.
He asks us to trust the Author.
The deeper message hidden within Exodus 4 is not merely about circumcision.
It is about covenant loyalty.
It is about the danger of compartmentalized faith.
It is about the impossibility of truly following God while reserving areas of life for ourselves.
The New Testament takes this truth even further.
Physical circumcision pointed toward a deeper spiritual reality.
Paul writes in Romans 2:29:
The Greek phrase is περιτομὴ καρδίας (peritomē kardias).
“Circumcision of the heart.”
God has always been after more than external compliance.
He desires transformed hearts.
Repentant hearts.
Surrendered hearts.
Hearts fully devoted to Him.
This is where the story suddenly becomes personal.
Most of us are not carrying an uncircumcised son through the wilderness.
But many of us carry hidden compromises.
Areas we explain away.
Areas we justify.
Areas we assume God will overlook because we are otherwise serving Him.
The terrifying beauty of Exodus 4 is that God loves His people too much to leave them there.
His confrontation is not rejection.
It is mercy.
His discipline is not abandonment.
It is love.
The same God who stopped Moses is the God who sent Moses.
The same God who confronted him is the God who used him.
The same God who threatened judgment is the God who delivered a nation through him.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Jesus Christ fulfilled perfectly what Moses never could.
Where Moses faltered, Christ obeyed.
Where Moses compromised, Christ remained faithful.
Where Moses deserved judgment, Christ bore judgment.
At the cross, holiness and mercy embraced.
Justice and grace met.
The One who had every right to condemn became the sacrifice that saves.
This is why the story ultimately points beyond Moses.
It points to Jesus.
The greater Deliverer.
The greater Mediator.
The greater Covenant Keeper.
And perhaps someone reading this today feels the weight of God's conviction.
Not condemnation.
Conviction.
You know there are places in your life where God has been calling you deeper.
You know there are areas where surrender has been delayed.
You know there are conversations you've avoided.
Habits you've protected.
Compromises you've excused.
Listen carefully.
The God who confronts is also the God who restores.
The God who exposes is also the God who heals.
The God who disciplines is also the God who redeems.
The lodging place was not the end of Moses' story.
It was the turning point.
What looked like destruction became preparation.
What looked like judgment became mercy.
What looked like scandal became grace.
Because that is what God does.
He takes broken people, confronts what must change, and rewrites their story for His glory.
Maybe that is your story too.
Maybe the place you fear most is actually where grace is waiting.
Maybe the confrontation you've resisted is the doorway to freedom.
Maybe the conviction you've been feeling is evidence that God has not given up on you.
And maybe, just maybe, the chapter that feels like the end is actually where redemption begins.
What area of your life has God been calling you to surrender?

The God who confronted Moses in the darkness was already preparing him for deliverance in the daylight.
